title: Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs

stories.title: 📜 Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs
summaryBullets: A pseudepigraphic collection of twelve speeches attributed to Jacob’s sons, composed c. 2nd century BCE, blending autobiography, ethical exhortations, and prophetic visions.
Each patriarch (e.g., Reuben, Simeon, Levi, etc.) recounts life events, warns against a particular vice or urges a virtue tied to his own story, then foretells his descendants' future.
Recurring structure: a personal testimony, moral instruction, and sometimes an apocalyptic or messianic prophecy—often closing with their death and burial.
Strong ethical emphasis: virtues like love, mercy, and truth are upheld; vices like pride, envy, fornication, and hatred are condemned. Joseph is repeatedly held up as the model of virtue.
Contains Sin–Exile–Return (SER) patterns, especially in Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Benjamin—each featuring confessions, exile imagery, and hope of return.
crossRefs: Genesis 49:1-28: Jacob calls his sons together to tell them what will befall them in the last days and speaks over each one in turn, praising, cursing and foretelling, which is the exact pattern these twelve speeches follow one son at a time.

Genesis 35:22: Reuben lies with Bilhah his father's concubine and Israel hears of it, one bare sentence with nothing added, which the first of these testaments turns into a confession running the length of a speech.

Genesis 34:25-31: Simeon and Levi take their swords and kill every male in Shechem after their sister is defiled, and Jacob answers that they have made him a stench to the inhabitants of the land, the day two of these testaments answer for.

Genesis 37:18-28: The brothers see Joseph coming, plot to kill him, strip him and throw him into a pit, and then sell him to a passing caravan for twenty pieces of silver, the act nearly every one of these testaments circles back to.

Genesis 39:7-12: Potiphar's wife takes hold of Joseph's garment day after day and he leaves it in her hand and runs out of the house, the scene that makes Joseph the model held up all through this collection.
Deuteronomy 33:1-29: Moses blesses the tribes one by one before he dies, naming each and saying what will come to it, the second model these farewell speeches are built on.

Deuteronomy 30:1-5: If Israel is driven out among the nations and turns back with all her heart, God will gather her from wherever she was scattered and bring her home, which is the cycle of sin, exile and return these testaments run again and again.

Acts 20:17-38: Paul calls the elders of Ephesus down to Miletus, tells them they will not see his face again, warns them what will come in after he goes, and kneels and prays with them on the shore, a farewell speech built to the same plan.

translationNotes.note: The word means a settled disposition and covers both a covenant and a will. A testament in this literature is a fixed form: the dying man calls his children, tells one episode from his own life, names the sin it exposed or the virtue it took, presses that on them, sometimes adds what he sees coming, gives orders about his burial, and dies. Genesis 49 sets the pattern and Deuteronomy 33 runs it again.

Head of a father's house, the founder a tribe traces itself back to. Acts 7:8 uses the word of the twelve sons of Jacob and Hebrews 7:4 uses it of Abraham. The twelve who speak here are Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Joseph and Benjamin, and they speak in that order.

The collection sets two spirits over every man, one of truth and one of deceit, and makes the choice between them the thing a life turns on. Deuteronomy 30:15-19 puts the same choice as life and good against death and evil, with the charge to choose life so that you and your offspring may live. 1 John 4:6 names the spirit of truth and the spirit of error in those words.

The adversary is called Beliar throughout this collection, and turning away from him is the standing charge in speech after speech. The Hebrew word means worthlessness, and the Old Testament uses it in set phrases for lawless men, as at Deuteronomy 13:13 where they are sons of Belial. 2 Corinthians 6:15 is the only place the New Testament uses the name, asking what agreement Christ has with Belial.

Several testaments run the same cycle: the tribe falls away, is carried off among the nations, and is brought back. It is the shape Moses lays down before Israel ever enters the land. Deuteronomy 30:1-5 states it whole, and Deuteronomy 28 sets out the blessings and the curses it turns on. These speeches restate the covenant's own terms one tribe at a time.

Rachel's maidservant, given to Jacob, and the mother of Dan and Naphtali at Genesis 30:1-8. Genesis 35:22 reports in one line that Reuben lay with her and that Israel heard of it, and adds nothing at all. Genesis 49:3-4 has Jacob strip the firstborn's place from Reuben for it. The first of these testaments builds an entire confession out of that single verse.

A secondary wife of lower standing whose children still counted to the house. Bilhah and Zilpah were given to Jacob on those terms and four of the twelve tribes descend from them, at Genesis 30:1-13. Taking a man's concubine was a public claim on his position, which is why 2 Samuel 16:21-22 has Absalom do it on the roof in the sight of all Israel.

A city in the hill country of Ephraim, sitting in the pass between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, and one of the most fought-over sites in Scripture. Genesis 34:25-31 has Simeon and Levi kill every male in it while the men were still sore from circumcision, and Jacob answer that they have made him stink among the people of the land. Genesis 49:5-7 has him curse their anger and scatter them in Israel.

The testament given to Levi is the longest in the collection and the most taken up with what is to come. Numbers 3:5-10 sets the tribe apart to serve the priests and keep the charge of the sanctuary, and Numbers 18:20-24 gives them the tithe in place of land because the LORD is their inheritance. Malachi 2:4-7 calls it the covenant of Levi and says the priest's lips should guard knowledge, since he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.

Semitic material standing behind part of this collection has actually been dug up. Copies of an Aramaic work about Levi were found at Qumran in Cave 1 and Cave 4, and further fragments of the same work came out of the Cairo Geniza at the end of the nineteenth century. A long Greek addition to the Testament of Levi in a manuscript at Mount Athos overlaps the same material, and a Hebrew Testament of Naphtali was also found at Qumran.

A geniza is the storeroom of a synagogue where worn-out writings are put away rather than destroyed, because anything carrying the divine name may not be thrown out. The one in the Ben Ezra synagogue in Old Cairo had been filling for roughly a thousand years when it was opened at the end of the nineteenth century, and it held something near three hundred thousand fragments, the Aramaic Levi material among them.

Bishop of Lincoln, who sent to Athens for a Greek copy of this collection and translated it into Latin in 1242. His own hand appears in notes throughout that codex, which survives at Cambridge. The Latin version circulated widely and made the book familiar across medieval Europe. Grosseteste read the passages that speak of Christ as genuine prophecy and charged that the book had been kept out of sight on account of them.

Joseph is held up in testament after testament as the pattern of chastity and of endurance under wrong. Genesis 39:7-12 has him leave his garment in Potiphar's wife's hand and run out of the house, Genesis 39:20-23 has him thrown into the prison and then put in charge of it, and Genesis 50:19-21 has him tell his brothers that they meant evil against him but God meant it for good.

The testament given to Asher is about the man who wears two faces, doing one thing openly and the opposite underneath, and calls him double-tongued. James 1:8 calls that man double-minded and unstable in all his ways, and James 4:8 tells the double-minded to cleanse their hands and purify their hearts. Matthew 6:24 puts it as the plain impossibility of serving two masters.

The word covers sexual immorality of every kind rather than one particular act. Reuben's testament opens on it and warns his sons against it at length, tying it back to what he did with Bilhah. Acts 15:29 puts abstaining from it into the short list the Jerusalem council sent out to the Gentile churches, and 1 Thessalonians 4:3 says the will of God is your sanctification, that you abstain from porneia.

The testament given to Dan is against anger and lying together, and it ties the two: the angry man cannot tell the truth about what he has done. Proverbs 14:29 says whoever is slow to anger has great understanding but the hasty-tempered exalts folly. Ephesians 4:26-27 says be angry and do not sin, do not let the sun go down on your wrath, and give no foothold to the devil.

stories.keyTakeaway: The Testaments present ethical and prophetic farewells from Jacob’s sons, urging moral fidelity and offering hope for restoration.

intro:
The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs are twelve farewell discourses, one for each son of Jacob, in the order Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Joseph, Benjamin. The pattern is the one set in Genesis 49, where Jacob calls his sons together to tell them what will befall them in the last days, and in the blessing of Moses in Deuteronomy 33. Each patriarch summons his children as he is dying, retells an episode from his own life as Genesis records it, names the vice it exposed or the virtue it required, presses that lesson on his descendants, often adds what he foresees for them, and dies. Reuben speaks on the sin with Bilhah and on fornication; Simeon on envy of Joseph; Levi on the priesthood; Judah on courage, wine, and love of money; Zebulun on compassion; Dan on anger and lying; Gad on hatred; Asher on the two faces a man can wear; Joseph, held up throughout the collection as the model, on chastity and endurance; Benjamin on the pure mind. Several of the testaments run a recurring cycle of sin, exile, and return.

The Greek text is known from fifteen manuscripts. The oldest complete one, Cambridge University Library MS Ff.1.24, was made in Constantinople in the late tenth or eleventh century, and its route into the West is documented. John of Basingstoke reported having seen a Greek copy in Athens in the library of the metropolitan Michael Choniates; Robert Grosseteste, bishop of Lincoln, sent for the manuscript, and in 1242 he translated it into Latin. His hand appears in notes throughout the codex. The Latin version circulated widely and made the book familiar in medieval Europe. An Armenian version survives in about fifty manuscripts and carries fewer of the Christian passages than the Greek does; Slavonic and Serbian versions also survive. Semitic material standing behind parts of the collection has been recovered. The Aramaic Levi Document was found at Qumran in Cave 1 (1Q21) and Cave 4 (4Q213-4Q214), and further fragments of it came out of the Cairo Geniza at the end of the nineteenth century, now held at Cambridge and Oxford; a long Greek addition to the Testament of Levi in a manuscript at Mount Athos overlaps the same material. A Hebrew Testament of Naphtali was also found at Qumran (4Q215).

The Greek text contains passages that speak plainly of Christ, and how those passages entered it is an open question with a long history and named positions. (1) Robert Grosseteste, in 1242, took the Greek to be a translation of a Hebrew original preserving the actual deathbed words of Jacob's sons, read the passages about Christ as genuine prophecy, and charged that the book had been kept out of sight on account of them. (2) Friedrich Schnapp, in 1884, argued that those passages are later Christian additions to a Jewish work, and R. H. Charles built on that in his 1908 edition, reconstructing a Jewish book of the second century BC overlaid with Christian interpolation. (3) Marinus de Jonge, from 1953 onward, argued that the Testaments as they stand are a Christian composition that drew on Jewish sources, and that no Jewish original can be recovered by deleting passages from the Greek. Two facts sit on the table for anyone weighing this: the Armenian version has fewer of the Christian passages than the Greek, and the Aramaic Levi material shows that Semitic sources behind at least the Testament of Levi existed before the Christian era.

No communion receives the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs as canonical.
